newsitem.title: FRANCE: Union says Jospin agrees EU farm plan unacceptable.
newsitem.headline: Union says Jospin agrees EU farm plan unacceptable.

text.p: The leader of France's largest farmers union branded proposals to cut European Union subsidies "unacceptable" on Wednesday and claimed the full support of the government.

"We must have new discussions and negotiations on this process...in which everyone is copying the Americans," FNSEA union leader Luc Guyau said after a one-hour meeting with Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.
"The prime minister took entirely the same position on this as we have," he said. Jospin's office made no statement.

The government said earlier that the Agenda 2000 plan, which aims to make European farmers more competitive by lowering prices towards world levels, would weaken the EU's bargaining position in the next round of global trade talks from 1999.

The Commission proposal to shift agriculture support from guaranteed prices and export subsidies to direct payments to farmers might also prove costly and disadvantage some farm sectors, French Agriculture Minister Louis Le Pensec said.
At present about 80 percent of ERU farm subisides go to just 20 percent of farmers.

European Commission President Jacques Santer unveiled the plan on Wednesday in Strasbourg. It aims to prepare for the entry of agriculturally backward east European states early next century and prevent a return of costly EU food surpluses.
In a statement, the FNSEA accused Santer of surrendering to American moves towards phasing out farm subsidies.
"Under the pretext of globalisation, the Commission is following the economic liberalism of the Anglo Saxons in a wide-eyed fashion," it said.
"It surrenders to our American competitors and the Cairns group countries even before negotiations begin," it said.
The broad-based FNSEA has traditionally had strongest relations with the centre-right which was ousted from power in a surprise parliamentary election defeat on June 1.
But analysts said the Socialists, while backing a ceiling on subsidies to wealthy grain farmers when in opposition, would tread carefully in one of the country's most sensitive arenas.
The government remembers how the last Socialist Paris administration was hounded from office in 1993 partly by violent farmers' protests over previous EU subsidy reforms.
Alientating farmers might also throw extra ammunition to conservative President Jacques Chirac, who has just clashed with Jospin over his constitutional role in domestic politics.

Weekly Le Canard Enchaine said Chirac, who robustly defends farmers and enjoys strong rural support, interrupted Le Pensec at a recent cabinet meeting to tell him to prevent Washington having the same domination over global farming as it does over economic and military affairs.
The United States last year introduced its most radical farm reforms since the 1930s Depression, known as the Fair Act, to allow its farmers a better chance to compete globally.
